utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Milan Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. With the permission of the Court, we would like to have our two assistants Ms. Maja Dokmanovic and Ms. Sipetic, Vanja present in the courtroom. We overlooked last week that we were supposed to ask for the permission of the Court that they sit. We sort of understood that the policy is that we can have our case managers and assistants as well in the courtroom. I'm sorry for this -- that we overlooked this, but I'm using this opportunity now to ask the Trial Chamber. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. They're allowed to sit in the courtroom as long as they're properly identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So they can sit in the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Prosecution is continuing examination-in-chief. Witness, you are still under solemn declaration and good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Before I continue examination-in-chief, may I raise two short questions? One is the Prosecution bench would just like to know whether or not we intend to sit this afternoon from 3.30 until 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It is the intention of the Trial Chamber, because we were informed by the Registrar that the facilities are there. So for now, we are sitting in the afternoon as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. The second issue is just a matter of a document which was disclosed to us on Friday by Defence counsel, and that document relates to this witness. And my understanding is that the Defence intend to use it in their cross-examination of this witness. Now, I'm not suggesting that the late disclosure of this was in any way a trick or anything, it was simply because, as is on the record, when exactly this witness would be heard was still very much up in the air. The consequence, however, is that one of those documents I've had -- didn't know existed. I had no chance to take any instruction on it. I've discussed with Defence counsel, and what I would like to ask the permission of the Chamber is whether during the break this morning one of the investigators from the Prosecution team could show that document to the witness, just ask about -- solely about that document and take instructions on it and then report back to me on that document. And I understand from the Defence this morning that they wouldn't oppose that way of proceeding if the Chamber was minded to grant permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I just want confirmation from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We don't object to that. That is right. The point was that we understood that Mr. Muhamed Bicic will take the stand first, and that is why we tried everything, with all our resources, to disclose these documents relating to Muhamed Bicic and only then it was changed to Hasan Bicic. That was why we disclosed it this late on Friday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. So the investigator will be allowed to get instructions from the witness on the document during the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Examined by Ms. Reidy: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bicic, on Friday we finished the session discussing an incident in which you told the Chamber you had been stopped at a checkpoint manned by personnel in JNA uniform, and you, and I believe your vehicle, had been searched. You also then began to tell the Chamber about information that you had been given from an acquaintance of yours that they had heard someone instruct the people at the checkpoint that you should be stopped and searched. On that point, I just want to clarify one or two matters. Can I ask you: Have you heard of a unit called the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you understand the 4th Detachment to be?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to define it now in a sentence, but I would say that it was an organised group of people, of uniformed individuals, who had some kind of training and organisation of their own, and it was common knowledge that their command, or headquarters, was in the AS Cafe, the proprietor of which was Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "uniformed men," what kind of uniform are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm talking about military uniforms. I think they were within the composition of the then Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said it was common knowledge that the headquarters was in Cafe AS, and that was owned by Mr. Tadic. Do you know whether any of the other defendants had a connection to the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Zaric was one of the commanders or organisers of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, again on Friday, you had -- I'm going to ask you one question: When did you become aware, if you can remember, about the existence of this so-called 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think several months prior to the conflict, before the war, before the occupation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Then on Friday you gave evidence that members of the 4th Detachment had been sitting in a cafe near a JNA checkpoint at Crkvina and that they were providing the persons manning the checkpoint with information as to who to stop.

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that from one of the locals from the village who was a client of mine - I don't remember his name - who used to come by my place. The young man told me seven days afterwards that he was present in the restaurant, he was in the restaurant - because it's a large restaurant which is called Trile - when one of the members of the 4th Detachment, whom I knew to be a member of the detachment, had said that they should stop me and search me because I probably had something on me that was of interest to them, but I don't think I had anything that would interest them.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have an objection. In the question, the Prosecutor said, "You said on --" "Then on Friday you gave evidence that members of the 4th Detachment had been sitting in a cafe near a JNA checkpoint," but in fact, the witness did not say that. He said members of the JNA, that they were members of the JNA. So could we clarify that? And in his answer, he said members of -- not members of the 4th Detachment, but other members. So could we clarify who was sitting -- who were the members at the checkpoint, sitting where they were?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sure the Prosecution have understood that and can seek clarification from the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bicic, the confusion appears to be the difference between the people who were at the checkpoint and the people who were sitting in the cafe where you -- that you were told about. I think it's clear from the record, but could you just once again emphasise for us: The people on the checkpoint, who were they? And then were also members of the 4th Detachment there? And then who were the people sitting in the cafe who you understand were passing intelligence information to the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was quite clear. I said that at the checkpoint there were persons in uniform, wearing the uniform of the JNA, whom I did not know. And it is also clear that I said that I was passed on information that there was information put out that I should be stopped and searched, and this was sent out by the members of the 4th Detachment who were in the restaurant called Trile, which is between Bosanski Samac and the checkpoint. And I think that's clear. I don't think there's any misunderstanding there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Thank you. I think that's now crystal clear. I'm going to ask you: In the -- this period before the 17th of April, were you a member of a political party at the time?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not a member of a political party, any political party up until then, but I did vote, and I can tell you that I voted for the SDA party. And the information there was accessible to one and all. So I was automatically in favour of the party, although I did not attend any of the party meetings except a founding session of the party, I think it was, with all the ethnic groups represented. I think that it took place in the Mitar Trifunovic memorial centre. But in principle, I was not a member of the party, neither did I take part in the work of the party or attend its party meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a member of any other organised group, for example, the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not a member of the Territorial Defence either, although I had heard that I was on some lists. Now, who compiled those lists and following whose orders, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have any discussions with anybody about joining the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that possibly there were some contacts but nothing official, no official meetings. And my agreement or anything like that was not the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this time, were you in possession of any weapons?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which weapons did you possess?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a pistol, which I came by legally with a permit from MUP. And later on, I bought two automatic rifles, one for my brother and one for myself, because that was the general trend. Everybody was arming themselves. And some people did so allegedly legally, that is to say, they were armed by the army or Territorial Defence, or they were themselves in a situation where they could seize weapons from the police and Territorial Defence. And when I say that, I mean the Serbs and some of their supporters, or if I can say so, sympathetic Muslims, Muslims who were sympathetic towards them. And on the other hand, the other side who was not able to come by any weaponry or take it from the Territorial Defence had to fend for themselves. They had to buy something on the black market in order to defend themselves from the aggression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said these two weapons which you acquired were from the -- what was your intention? What did you intend to do with these weapons, having illegally acquired them?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, we procured those weapons so that if the need arose, we could defend our homes and families and town. And also at that time, you could buy a bomb at the marketplace, just like pears or apples or eggs, whatever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do I take it that you had one pistol which was licensed, two newly acquired automatic rifles? Was that the extent of the weapons that were in your home, or did you have other weapons?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had other weapons as well; a pistol. My brother had a pistol, and he came by it the same way that I did, with a -- legally licensed from the MUP. He was a hunter, and he had a hunting rifle as well. And that would be all. Those were the weapons we had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you had acquired the weapons, the two automatic rifles, with the intention of defending yourself if it came to that. Who were you going to defend, yourself or your family living with you at the time in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your family remain with you in Bosanski Samac up until the night of the takeover?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Luckily, no, they didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were your family at the time of the takeover?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some five or six days before this, before the takeover of power, I -- as luck would have it, I transferred my family across the border to Croatia to stay with friends.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What made you to decide then to take your family to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first and foremost, it was the wartime psychosis that prevailed, and then the general events. I'm speaking about the explosions that took place and the situation in general, the barricades that had been erected. Quite simply, there was this aura of war. You could feel the smell of war, in fact. And I wasn't the only one to evacuate my family. The Serbs had done that even before me, and I think some Croats as well. They took their families away; the first to Serb villages, the second to Croatian villages or to Serbia proper in Croatia. But nobody had to tell me this, because there was a general feeling in town. The town had become practically empty, and you could see this especially at night. You could see where the lights were on in the windows and where they weren't in the neighbouring houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With all this general, as you call it, war psychosis, were there meetings held in the community to try to discuss what was happening?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were probably quite a few of those meetings, but I remember attending one particular meeting and that was held outside in the open air, in a town square, and I think it was approximately seven days before the occupation of Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us who spoke at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several speakers. I can't remember them all now, but I do remember that amongst them were Mr. Simo Zaric, Borislav Pisarevic, an elderly lady. She was a Muslim whose sons were in the Serb police force. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I can't remember her name. So there were quite a number of people who spoke at that -- well, let's call it meeting, rally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what exactly was the contents of the speeches made at that rally? Or not exactly, but in general, what was the message that the speakers were trying to give to those assembled?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it ran along the following lines: that there will not be a war, that people should not flee, that tensions were quietening down. And quite simply, what I thought they were doing was trying to say that there would be no war. That would be the gist of it and the message from that rally, as I saw it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you believe the message?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, luckily I did not believe it, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what did you do, then, after this rally, even though you had been told that there had been no reason to get worried about impending war?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believed -- well, just to show how much I believed the meeting was that, that very night I transferred my family out of there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you testified that this meeting took place approximately a week before the takeover. I'd like to bring you now to the events on the 16th and 17th of April. Do you remember what you were doing on the 16th of April in 1992?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that day. I think on that day, or rather, that evening, the war psychosis has reached its culmination. And I had my customary working day. And sometime towards evening, or perhaps 8.00 or 9.00 in the evening - that was the peak period for our catering enterprise - usually it was jammed with customers. But this time there were only five or six customers, and you couldn't see anybody in the streets. There were no passersby. Everybody seemed to have either left Samac or withdrawn to their own homes, stayed at home in their flats or houses. And in one of the large buildings, on the left-hand side, opposite my pizzeria - it was an apartment building with about 20 apartments - I saw that at that time, only three -- there were lights on in only three of the apartments in the building. And this war psychosis, quite simply, and the atmosphere that prevailed in town had reached a peak. There was so much tension and nervousness around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you had only very few customers in your pizzeria that evening. Did you have any particular discussions or conversations with anyone about why there were so few people that particular evening?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were outside, in front of the pizzeria. It was around 9.00 in the evening. I think there were a few people sitting inside. I was standing outside with someone, and of course, the topic of our conversation was the wartime psychosis and everything accompanying it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you remain in your pizzeria that evening?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I closed it early that evening, very early.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go after you had closed your pizzeria?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, I went home. But I would like to add something before I locked up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At one point - it was around 9.00 p.m., when I was chatting with my neighbours and some of my customers in front of my pizzeria - a neighbour of mine from the building I mentioned across from my pizzeria, on the left-hand side, approached me to a distance of about five metres and called me to one side. His name was Mladen Jordic. I knew him from before. Our parents were acquaintances. He called me to one side, and he asked me what was going on. He said, "What's going on, neighbour? You wouldn't shoot at me, would you?" I think I replied that I assumed he knew what was going on and that I wouldn't shoot at anyone, nor would I shoot at him, and that I wasn't interested in that at all. I think he knew what was about to happen, just as I did. I mention this because of some events that followed later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Before you provide us with that testimony, you said that you had, I think, closed your pizzeria and that you had gone home. Can you tell us, then, how the events of that evening unfolded, as best as you can recall?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, nothing special, until about perhaps 3.00 a.m., when detonations were heard from various directions around the town, and perhaps in the town itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do when you heard, what you called, detonations?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I thought that the war had really started. After that, I went out onto the balcony, and I saw that some of my neighbours were already out in the street. They all looked very disturbed, upset. And so I also went out in front of my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- when you went outside of your house, did you discover any information that could tell you what was going on?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were various rumours going around. There was speculation. But I thought -- well, I think there was panic. I think there was quite a lot of disinformation, information people heard on the phone from various parts of town, so that there was fear among the people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what did you do? Did you stay outside in front of your house with your neighbours, or did you do something else?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We stayed there for quite some time. I don't know how many hours. And after that, I went as far as the town centre to try to see for myself what was going on. But as I said, there was general panic. The explosions and shooting were quite loud. People started panicking, and I think many people used that day or that afternoon to flee from the town. I think they had an opportunity to flee through Bosnia, or rather, over the bridge on the River Bosna, which had not yet been destroyed. And after that, I think they found ways to flee to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand that night was quite panicky. After you'd been downtown and that, what did you do for the rest of that night and morning?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in two minds as to whether I should flee or whether I should stay in my house. I tried discussing this situation and both options with my brother, but -- unfortunately, we decided to stay at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you just stay at home and wait, or did you try to find out further information as to what was going on?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I stayed. I don't know myself what I was waiting for, but I stayed at home thinking I had a right to stay at home. And after some time, I tried to get some information about what was really going on in our town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you try to get that information?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to think about who I could call and who could give me correct information, someone who was influential, someone I knew and who knew me, and then I phoned. I decided to call Mr. Borislav Pisarevic, and I talked to him about the situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just clarify for the record? You said you called someone that you knew. How did you know Mr. Pisarevic previously?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Pisarevic was a very well-known lawyer, and he used to represent me as well. Apart from that, he was a customer of mine. So we knew each other, and I had no reason not to trust him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you called Mr. Pisarevic, what was he able to tell you?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Pisarevic told me that as far as he knew, the best thing to do would be to stay calm. He said that weapons were being collected from people and that if we had any weapons, we should hand them over to the army, the police, or someone who was collecting weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When exactly, or as close, can you remember did you make the telephone call to Mr. Pisarevic?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you exactly now, but I think it was late in the afternoon on that day when the occupation of our town began. I think it was in the late afternoon or perhaps the early evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "that day," do you mean the 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you follow Mr. Pisarevic's advice?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I had no choice. The detonations were already coming from all directions, from my street as well, and it was too dangerous to go outside. So I simply obeyed and stayed at home, waiting for someone to come and collect the weapons and to hand over our weapons to them. I had the impression that the town was completely occupied and that there was even fighting, although later I heard that there had been no fighting but only intimidation and simply occupation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to you, on the telephone Mr. Pisarevic said you should prepare your weapons. You testified you had a number of weapons in your home. What did you do with those weapons?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing. The weapons were in the room. I was with my brother in his apartment in our family house, and we waited. We simply waited. We felt great uncertainty. Throughout the night, we were waiting to see what would happen, and this feeling of expectation was mixed with fear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did someone come to collect the weapons?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They came on the following day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened when people came to collect the weapons?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the following day, that is, on the 18th of April - I think it was in the morning; I don't remember exactly at what time - we heard especially strong detonations around our house. We had already pulled down all the blinds so that we didn't know what was going on outside. But by the sound, we concluded that -- or, rather, by the sound of vehicle engines, we thought that there were armoured vehicles. And by the sound of the detonations, we thought they were large-calibre weapons. So on the 18th of April, in the morning, I had the feeling that our house was surrounded. And they were yelling very loudly - I think they even had a loudspeaker - telling us to open the door, that they were coming for our weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you open the door?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, in fact, the weapons were lying on the floor in the room. Neither of us wanted to use the weapons. I think we had no chance. We tried to open the door, but as we were trying to open it, when we had opened it only a crack, the people in uniform - I don't recall what uniforms they were, but I think they were all in military uniforms - kicked the door in, and at the same moment they hit my brother with a rifle butt. He fell down. And they pushed me. They didn't hit me, but they pushed me, and I fell. They ordered me to get up, and they put a knife to my throat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you think these people were in military uniform. Did you recognise any of them?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said they were all in military uniform, but I was unable to recognise any of them. Some of them wore masks and some had paint on their faces so that their faces were black or -- well, they were covered with paint, olive-grey. I think it was more black, black paint. I didn't know any of them, or at any rate, I couldn't recognise anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said they had hit your brother and they had a knife at your throat. What else did they do? Did they ask you questions? Did they take any further action?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, before they asked any questions, they did all this with a lot of cursing. They cursed our Ustasha and balija mothers, threatening to kill us, to cut our throats, or both. They asked for valuables. And while some of them were holding us - and they had a knife to my throat, and my brother was lying on the floor with an automatic rifle pointed at his head - they asked where we kept our gold jewellery, our money. And while they were questioning us like this, others were already ransacking the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they do with the weapons which you say you had laid out on the floor?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as we were able to talk and explain that some of these weapons were legally held, that we had licences from the MUP and so on, we tried, but I think this did not have any effect. I think they were very happy about the pistols, because they wanted them. They were vying with each other as to who should get them. I think they had a high value on the market. They were good pistols.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The pistols are the ones which were the legal weapons?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were pistols we had bought on the legal market, with a licence from the MUP, and at that time people held them in high regard. I think they were called CZ-99. They were produced domestically, but they were very good pistols, and I think they wanted to keep them. Anyway, they took all our weapons and they beat us, so I wasn't paying attention to the weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When they beat you, what were they using to beat you?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they beat us with rifle butts and they also kicked us, and they had boots on their feet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did they kick you or hit you with the rifle butt?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All over my body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you sustain injuries from these kicks and hits?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did, but at that moment I don't think I felt any pain, because the situation was to survive or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified that these military persons were wearing -- had masks or painted faces. Could you recognise anything about them, though, for example, through their accents?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was unable to recognise anyone. As I said, some of them wore masks and others had their faces painted. But it was very characteristic - and I recognised this, I couldn't help but recognise it - and that was their dialect, the dialect they used to speak to each other. It was purely Serbian dialect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did all the people speak with this dialect or only some of the people?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the ones who spoke and who at that moment were looting or beating us, that they used a Serbian dialect from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the events you described, did the -- the soldiers, did they leave?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't leave. They pushed us out, out of our house, battered as we were. In front of the house, a white Golf was parked. They pushed us into that Golf, and I think there were three soldiers with us. They put me in the back seat between two soldiers. One was driving. My brother was sitting in front. They pointed guns or, rather, pistols at both of us. A pistol Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was -- there was a pistol against my forehead and another one against the back of my brother's neck, and then they drove us away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were driving away, did you know where they were going to take you?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know where they were taking us, but I began to think. I thought this was the end and that they were taking us to the River Sava to shoot us there, because that was the direction we were driving in approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they in fact take you to the River Sava, or did you end up somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took us, and it was in the direction of the Sava, but they took us to the front of the police station, the MUP station in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could I ask if the usher would mind placing before the witness the Exhibit 9 -- P9D, which was marked by the witness on Friday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bicic, I was wondering, in front of you marked with the number "1" and "2" the location of your house and pizzeria, if possible, could you mark with a number "3" the SUP building where you say you were taken in the white Golf. If you could use the pen and mark that on the map.

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, as far as I can find my way on this map, I have marked the place where the police station was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So you were taken to the SUP in the white Golf. Can you please tell the Chamber what happened upon your arrival at the SUP?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we arrived at the police station, I noticed a large group of people in uniforms. I think there might have been even as many as 30 of them. They ordered us to get out of the car and said that we were to go into the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do I take it that you went into the police station?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We wanted to go in. That was what they had ordered us to do. But in the meantime, this group of soldiers or these people wearing uniforms lined up in front of the entrance to the police station. They made a sort of line, and we had to go through this line on either side of us to go into the police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could I ask the usher, would the usher mind showing the witness Exhibit P14A, number 43.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can see in front of you, is this the building that you were taken to in the white Golf?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's the building. It's the police station in Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you mind just pointing out on the photograph where exactly these men were when you said they lined up and you were to go between them?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that they were in front of the police station, and this double line was at the entrance itself. This is the door, and they were lined up in two columns here, and we had to pass between them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you said you had to go through this line. Did they beat you or do anything else to you whilst you were going through this line?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Counsel, avoid leading questions, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I'll rephrase that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you went through the line into the police station. Could you tell us if anything happened on your way into the police station.

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had to run the gauntlet. And from the first man to the last man, they took advantage of this and seized the opportunity to beat us. And while beating us, they swore at us, cursed us, and so forth. They beat us all over our bodies with whatever they had at hand, with their rifles. And if one of us would fall from the blow he had received or the pain, they would proceed to kick us and make us get up. So we had to pass through and to run the gauntlet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said they swore at you and cursed you. What sort of swearing and cursing was that?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The usual kind of swear words that they used. They cursed our Ustasha mothers, our balija mothers, and sometimes our Muslim mothers as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you had finished running the gauntlet, what happened to you then? I presume at this stage you were in the SUP.

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we succeeded in passing through this double line, in the corridor inside the SUP building, I met Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was Mr. Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic was -- well, I was to learn later on, in fact, that he was the head of the Serb police, chief of police of that part that they had taken control of through the occupation. But otherwise, I knew him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You knew Mr. Todorovic before this meeting at the SUP entrance; is that -- that's correct?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did know him, yes, well. He was a frequent customer in my pizzeria.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What -- or did anything -- did anything happen when you met Mr. Todorovic in the corridor inside the SUP building?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I tried to ask him, as I assumed that he held some sort of function and that he wielded some sort of influence, what was actually going on, what was happening to us and why, why we had been brought there and why they were behaving towards us in the way that they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get an answer from Mr. Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. His answer was somewhat unusual. Todorovic's answer was a little unusual.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his answer?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said something that first came into his head, I think. He wanted to accuse us. What he said was, "Keep quiet and don't ask any questions. In your pizza bar, the HDZ members meet regularly." And that was quite absurd, because first of all, I myself am a Muslim; second of all, members of all the ethnic groups frequented my catering establishment. So the answer to me seemed to be ridiculous. Looking at it -- looking back at it now, I thought it was rather unusual for him to say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After he had given you the answer, did he leave you alone?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He went off, or I think he did, whereas my brother and I were separated into two different rooms, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the ground floor. They took me off to an office, and there was a big wooden, heavy writing desk in that office. On the desk, there was a plate of glass which was broken, and the fragments of that broken glass were on the table, on the desk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you entered this office?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had my back turned towards the door, and at one point I suddenly felt that I just had to turn around, and I did. I turned around to see what had made me want to turn around.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you turned around, what had made you want to turn around?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that particular moment, I happened to see my neighbour, Mladen Djordjic, who was nodding his head, and said, "Yes, that's him."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the same person who you had met outside your pizzeria on the evening of the 16th?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the same person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you had spotted your neighbour, what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They started beating me, and they ordered me to take my clothes off, to strip completely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who started beating you?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the men who were in the room. I didn't dare turn around, nor could I.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many men did you get the impression were in the room?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the impression that there were at least three or four of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell if they were civilians, soldiers, police officers?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that particular moment, I wasn't -- I don't know who beat me. Probably those people in uniforms. Whether they were policemen or soldiers, I don't know. But I don't think there were any civilians among them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you said that they ordered you to take your clothes off, to strip. And did you follow their instructions?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you had to follow their instructions. Yes, I did. I took my clothes off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then what did you do?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They ordered me to lie down on my stomach, to lie across the table, over this broken glass.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I lay down on the table, they continued to beat me all over my body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, do you have any impression about what they were using to hit you with?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- that is to say, while I was lying there on the table, I thought they were hitting me with police batons mostly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any idea how long this beating went on for?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it for a very long time or a short time? Just roughly, any idea?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not -- somewhere in between that, not too long and not too short.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the beating did finish, again, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then they ordered me to put my clothes back on again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you sustained any specific injuries or cuts from the beating you had endured?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't pay attention to that at all. I think that the state I was in at that moment, my psychological state and all the fear that I experienced, was too great to be able to tell you precisely now whether I had cuts or whatever. I didn't think about that, didn't have time to think about that at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've mentioned your psychological state. Do I take it -- could you just explain to us briefly what was your psychological state at that time.

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult now, after so much time, to describe my state, but what I can say is that I felt very, very bad. I felt as if they would either cut our throats or shoot us or massacre us in some way at that very moment. I felt very degraded and hurt and all beaten up, and all that together; I felt all these things at the same time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you had put your clothes back on, what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I got dressed, I saw that my brother was close by. I think they took me out again, and we probably met in the corridor of the police station, on the ground-floor level, and they ordered the guards to take us away to a room up on the floor above.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you and your brother were put into a room on the first floor. Did you stay there for the rest of the day, or how long did you stay in this room for?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We stayed in that room on the first floor until nightfall. I'm not sure what time it was, but until the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in there by yourselves?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they threw us into the room, there was just myself and my brother. We were alone. They placed one or two guards - when I say "one or two," what I mean is that sometimes there were two guards at the door, sometimes just one - and they had not a mask on their faces, but they had a sort of camouflage paint on their faces. And I heard them very clearly ordering these guards that if we put a foot wrong, that they should shoot at us and aim at our heads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you went into the room, you were alone. Did you remain alone until nightfall?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I don't know the order in which this happened, but they brought some other people into the room that we were in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did they bring into the room, even if you don't get it in the chronological order?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted) (redacted) an old Albanian - his name was Ramadan Simnica - and a third person whose name was Sulejman Tihic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you and the other people who were put into the room, were you left alone during the day to your own devices, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were guarded the whole time, and the people who came in to beat us would take turns, so that we had several visits by different people. I don't remember by how many, but there were many people who came in visiting, with different intentions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us -- could you describe for us some of these visits paid by people?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for example, some people came in just to beat us and swear at us and curse us and humiliate us. Some did the same thing, but they also freed us or rid us of our gold chains, the gold chains that we had round our necks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of cursing and swearing would that be?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, while they were beating us, because we were sitting down on the floor, they would swear at us, and the usual swear word they used was that they would curse our Ustasha mothers or balija mothers or Muslim mothers, things of that kind. And then they would curse our president, and they mentioned Alija Izetbegovic. They had a broad span of swear words and curses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that they freed you of your gold chains. Did you want to be freed of your gold chains?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if we wanted to be relieved of them or not. Probably not. But as my brother was sitting closest to the door, they noticed a gold chain round his neck first, and I think one of them pulled it off my brother's neck, pulled it over his head. And we were paid a visit by two individuals at this point. I didn't know them, but judging by their accent and the type of swear words they used, especially I was sure that they were Serbs from Serbia. And then they happened to see the chain round my own neck just after that, so that they each tried to seize the chain from me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they succeed in taking your chain?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the first attempt, because they weren't able to break the chain, so that they pulled my head along with it. Both of them held onto the chain firmly and pushed my head downwards so that I had the feeling Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that they could pull my ears off together with the chain. Luckily though, I wasn't tied at that particular moment. So I helped them relieve me of my chain and take it off over my head, and I was happy that my ears had remained intact. When they succeeded in getting the chain off over my head, I had the feeling -- that is to say, they started a tug-of-war with the chain to see who would get it, and I almost had the feeling that they were about to shoot each other over this chain they were squabbling so much. They didn't beat us too much on that occasion because I think they were satisfied with the gold chains that they had managed to seize. When I say "they," I mean the two of them, our two visitors, the two men that had paid us a visit at that particular time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anything else taken from you that day in the room?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not that day in that room, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that day, did you receive any sustenance, any food, any water? Were you allowed to go to the toilet?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We weren't allowed to do anything. They didn't give us any food or water, nor were we allowed to go to the toilet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say you stayed there until nightfall. Where were you -- where did you go to at nightfall?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it was night-time, they transferred us to the Territorial Defence, the warehouse of the Territorial Defence in fact, which was just across the road. But may I just say one more thing in relation to the room we were in at the police station, if I may?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Briefly speaking, when they brought Mr. Sulejman Tihic into the room we were in, a man appeared wearing a uniform. I think he was wearing a camouflage uniform, in fact, but a military uniform, at any rate. And I was to come to know that man well later on. They referred to him by the nickname of Lugar. I didn't know who he was at the time, but he took advantage of the occasion and introduced himself to us straight away. He did this by beating us all up in that short space of time. He beat us with a police baton, but only on our heads and in our faces, not on our shoulders or backs. At one particular moment, he took up the telephone. And there was still telephone communication. It was still working. And I think he called up Serbia. I think he was calling his wife or his girlfriend or someone like that, anyway. He had a brief conversation with the woman, and then he ordered Sulejman Tihic to kneel down beside him, and he beat him on his face with the baton while speaking into the telephone mouthpiece. He was saying, "Listen to the president crying." Sulejman Tihic was the president of the Party of Democratic Action in Bosanski Samac. That's just a detail that I wanted to recount.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can I ask you: How did it make you feel to watch the president of the Party of Democratic Action being beaten and made to cry out loud?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to put it in a nutshell, I felt completely helpless, and I was in a very sorry state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the witness has just testified that he was moved to the Territorial Defence warehouse, and I would seek to go through to his evidence as to what happened when he was transferred there. But maybe, giving that it's close to 11.00, I would hold my questions until after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take a break now and resume our proceedings at 1130 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution is continuing.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bicic, just before the recess, you had testified to the fact that you were transferred to the Territorial Defence building around nightfall.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could I -- again, could I just ask that the witness be given Exhibit 9D.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for completion's sake, Mr. Bicic, could you mark with a number "4" on the map where this Territorial Defence warehouse was where you were taken.

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So I can see from the map, it's across the road. When you were taken across the road, what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many guards or armed persons took us across the road, beating us along the way. And they pushed us into a room. I think it used to be a storeroom belonging to the Territorial Defence. As far as I can remember, this was the first room on the left-hand side, and it had a metal door and bars on the upper part.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I ask the usher, could you show the witness P14A, number 2, number 50 and number 5. Perhaps number 2 of that exhibit could be just placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bicic, could you just tell us from the photograph what is in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Straight ahead is the police station, and the yard belongs to the Territorial Defence. On the right-hand side is the building, on the right. May I indicate it? If necessary, I can. I'm referring to this building here. This is the Territorial Defence warehouse, and a little to the right there is a metal door leading into the room where we spent the following ten days or so.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Could I ask the usher, could you please place number 5 on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bicic, do you recognise what is now depicted in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell the Chamber what is depicted there?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entrance to the room where we were locked up and the door of that room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those are the doors which you indicated in the previous photograph as having been on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm finished with the photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I understand you were taken to the room shown on the photograph that evening. Was the room empty?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't empty. There were, as far as I can estimate, between 20 and 30 people in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know who any of those 20 or 30 people were?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew most of them very well. They were people from the town of Samac. Most of them were good acquaintances of mine, and just like us, most of them were in a very sorry state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "very sorry state," what exactly do you mean by that description?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean by this that many of them were bloody and they had visible injuries to the head. They were battered, like me, and they looked pitiful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said these were persons from the town of Bosanski Samac. Do you know the ethnicity of the people in the room?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say they were persons from the town, I also meant -- I really meant the municipality of Samac. They were from the surrounding villages as well. And as for their ethnic composition, they were about 50/50 Muslims and Croats. Perhaps at that moment the ratio was 60 per cent Muslims, 40 per cent Croats, but on the whole, I would say it was 50/50.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall if there was any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Excuse me. Oh, yes. Maybe I will allow that question before I seek clarification.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I ask if there were any persons of Serb ethnicity detained with you in that room?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think at that moment it wasn't easy for me to distinguish Serbs from Croats because up until then, we had never really focused on these differences. But I think there was at least one man of Serb ethnicity. His name was Dragan. I can't remember his last name, but I remember his nickname. Dragan Mirin they called him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted to find out, of the people that you found in the room, the ones that were battered like you, the ones that were in a sorry state and yourself, was there any one of them in military uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember seeing any of them in military uniform, but there were a few of them in police uniforms or uniforms of the reserve police force or something like that, or I think the regular police. I'm not referring to the Serb police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bicic, when you were put into this room, could you then tell us what happened -- if anything happened that evening or if anything happened the next day?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing special. There was nothing special that made it different from other evenings. The evenings were all the same. We had frequent visits by armed men, especially in the first days. We were frequently beaten, tortured, maltreated, and humiliated, so that I can say that there was no difference actually between the evenings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bicic, I would like to question you some more about what you mean when you say you were frequently beaten, tortured, and maltreated, but could you first tell us, roughly over how many days were you kept in the Territorial Defence warehouse?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my estimation, about ten days. Maybe it was ten, but about ten. That's as precise as I can be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you testified that you were frequently beaten, tortured, and maltreated, and I'd like you now to tell us a little bit about some of these beatings. Could you tell me, just even at whatever estimation, how frequently, how many times a day or in the evening you would estimate you were beaten?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let us say in the first days, I was taken to the police station every day to make some sort of statements. Of course I assumed that the territory we were on had been declared Serb territory. I had to write these statements in the Cyrillic alphabet. But I think I managed that. At every interrogation or giving of a statement, they were very, very cruel. They frequently - I'm referring to the following days - they frequently took us out into the Territorial Defence yard, two or three at a time, and they took us to different parts of the yard and beat us. Each one of us was beaten simultaneously by at least three uniformed men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I just ask you to concentrate on the interrogations for the moment. You said that also during the interrogations they were very cruel. Whilst you were actually being interrogated, was someone hitting you at that time?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this was the usual procedure at the time. Beating always accompanied interviews. On the first or second day -- I think it was the first. That was the day after we were taken to the Territorial Defence warehouse. Two guards arrived and said they had to take me to the police station to make a statement. As I was crossing the road, at that very moment a vehicle I knew stopped in front of the police station. This was my jeep. And a gentleman, the one who had beaten Sulejman Tihic the previous day, came out of it. They took me upstairs in the police station. They brought me into a room into which two armed men entered. I later learnt that one of them was called Laki, and I got to know him later. It was characteristic that he had only two or three fingers on one hand, and that's how I recognised him afterwards. And I think his last name was Lazarevic, and he was known as Laki. There were two of them, I think. And on that occasion, they beat me, as always. The only difference was that one of them - I don't recall which one - put the barrel of his pistol into my mouth and pushed it as far as it could go, and I was sure that he would damage my teeth. He demanded that I give them the keys to my car, my Mercedes. When I was brought into that room, I saw a crate of whiskey in a corner and another crate with 50 packets of cigarettes, 50 packs. I had two storerooms full of those goods. These were goods from my pizzeria. They opened a bottle of whiskey in front of me and toasted each other, and then they started questioning me and maltreating me and, of course, beating me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me, when they were -- again, when they were beating you, what did they use to beat you with?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was hit several times on the head with that same pistol, but I think that during that interrogation, they did not concentrate on beating me. The purpose of this interrogation was different. I mean, they were trying to get some material benefit, to extort things from me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that during this interrogation, that you saw bottles of your own whiskey and cigarettes which originated from your pizzeria. How did you know that those goods were from your pizzeria?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somebody had written "AS" [as interpreted] on the outside of the boxes, and that was the name of my establishment.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The witness said his nickname was Hase, H-a-s-e. It's not "AS"; it's "Hase." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can you clarify that, Madam Prosecutor, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bicic, could you just clarify for us what was -- what the name was that was written on the outside of the boxes.

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can spell it for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That would be helpful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: H-a-s-e, Hase. And that is my nickname, of course. It's short for my name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You said this interrogation was not concentrated on beating you. Was it these same people who used to interrogate you every time you and -- took over, or did other people also sometimes interrogate you?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they changed very often, and each of them asked different questions or had different motives for taking me to be interrogated, to make statements, and everything else that accompanied this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've mentioned before that these statements were in Cyrillic. Were you forced to handwrite the statements yourself, or was someone else typing up these statements?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had to write them out myself in my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would they ask you a question and you would write down the answer, or how did it go that you came to make these statements?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that most of those who interrogated us had not been trained to question people, and each of them said that he was a Serbian inspector or policeman. But the questions were different, and so were the methods of questioning. Sometimes they would give me a piece of paper and a pen and say, "Write down everything you know." It was hard to understand their questions and it was hard for me to ask questions of them, because we were maltreated and beaten every time we were interrogated. They cursed us. They humiliated us. And all this accompanied the interrogations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you at any stage recognise any of the people or know any of the people who were interrogating you?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were frequently beaten and interrogated, but this happened mostly in the first few days, where most of the interrogators were the people from Serbia. I and a few of us got to know them, got to remember them during the first two days really well, because we were really afraid of them. Sometimes I had the feeling that the local policemen were also afraid of these people. They were very cruel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. During your interrogations or your transfer to the SUP, did you ever see any local policemen around?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Very often, especially when we were questioned in the police station. I saw some inspectors and some policemen whom I knew from before, so I frequently saw local people there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During these -- you testified that the subject matter of the interrogation would sometimes be different, and you gave one example where it was in the room where your whiskey and cigarettes were. What were the other sort of questions or information that they wanted from you, apart from where your car was?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, only during that interrogation, I think they wanted to get hold of some loot or something like that. But in most of my statements, most of the interrogations, questions were asked such as: Where did you get your weapons? Who did you supply with weapons? I was accused of being a member of the Party of Democratic Action and that I had armed people. I was told that I was a member of the Territorial Defence and that I had armed people, that I had given money to procure weapons. The accusations were all in that direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me -- well, you've said that sometimes you were given a paper and told to write down what you know. Were you forced to sign any statements that were taken during these interrogation sessions?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regularly. I regularly signed the statements. Yes, I regularly signed them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So I will leave the topic of the interrogations, and perhaps you could take us back to the description of your conditions whilst you were in detention in the Territorial Defence warehouse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Counsel, before we leave this question of signing these statements which he was making, I think we need more information on them. Did he read them or were they read to him? Did he agree with the contents of those statements? And when he says he regularly signed them, there can be a confusion with what he means by "regularly signing." It could be a regular procedure or an irregular procedure. Can we have clarification, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bicic, before -- again, to go back to the statements that were taken in these interrogation sessions, would you say -- when you say that you regularly signed them, what exactly do you mean that you regularly signed statements?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant that I had to write a statement and when I finished it, that I had to sign it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you signed the statement, were you given time to read the statement, or was it read out aloud to you?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually, usually I didn't even know what I had written or, actually, I wasn't in a position to know what I had written. In addition to the questions about weapons, they asked me -- well, they didn't ask me. They made me make up lists of people who I was in an organisation with. And when I said that I was in no organisation at all, then they would beat me especially after that. So I had to compile some kind of list, some lists. I had to write down something. I think that I tried to write down the names of people whom I assume or whom I was certain were not there so as not to put these people in the same position that I was in. But I was forced to write down something. I had to write down some names. I had to write -- make up some lists.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say you were forced to, if you hadn't written anything down or if you had refused to sign a statement, what would have been the consequence?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said on several occasions that for each statement that we gave at that time to the Territorial Defence, I would be beaten and abused and all the rest of it. And then I realised that it would be better for me to comply and to write something down and so satisfy my interrogators at least for that one time, to take it time by time. I thought that it would be better to write down something, rather than nothing at all. I don't think I had any great choice in the matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. REIDY
utterances.text: Your Honour, do you want some more?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. So would you say that of all the statements that you were made to write down and sign? Did they contain what the people who were interrogating you wanted to say, or did they contain any truths according to your own knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was something that they wanted to hear or which could have proved satisfactory for the time being. I had to write down something to do with the question I was asked. So when they asked me about weapons, on many occasions I had to write down that I, too, had procured two rifles illegally. And I gave a lot of statements on that topic and received many beatings. But I also had to compile lists of people who had allegedly belonged to some supposed organisation, that I was a member, because most of my interrogators were accusing me of being -- they said that my name was on some lists, lists of people or organisations, and I think they considered them to be their enemies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Now, of the people whom you listed to belong to these organisations, was that the correct information, that these people you listed actually belonged to any of those organisations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that they were certainly members of some of those organisations, because let me tell you, I had to be convincing because it was a matter of life and death for me. So I had to write down some names, the name of some of the people that they knew belonged to the organisation, some of those organisations, and that I knew, those sort of compromised organisations allegedly, so that I assumed that some of the people that I wrote down were safe. When I say "safe," that they weren't in custody or in town. So I tried to get round it in that way and list some of those whom I assumed to be somewhere safe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Mr. Bicic, what sort of organisations are you referring to? What types?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if I used the right term when I said "organisation," but they seemed to imply that I was on the list of members of the Democratic Action Party, for example, and the newly formed Territorial Defence of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or something along those lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Those are the two they had in mind, the Territorial Defence and the Democratic Action Party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bicic, were you ever shown -- you said that they accused you of being a member of these organisations. Were you ever shown these lists where your name was alleged to have been found?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see those lists, but I heard on many occasions and in the course of many interrogations and beatings that they would always mention these lists where my name allegedly figured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But at no stage were you confronted with those lists; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. As far as I remember, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Bicic, now I will turn to, as I said, the conditions and occurrences in the Territorial Defence building. You said that at the beginning you were taken daily for interrogations. Whilst you were in the Territorial Defence warehouse, what were the conditions? Were you left alone when you weren't being interrogated?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that when they threw us into that warehouse building or the warehouse of the Territorial Defence, there might have been some 30 people there at the time. But over the next few days, new people would be brought in on a daily basis. So at the end, there were 40 or more of us in one room which was about 40 square metres in size, I would say. As to the conditions, the conditions were inhuman to begin with. We were on a concrete floor, totally unhygienic conditions. We were beaten daily. Me and a few others were slightly privileged to have three beatings a day, as many as three beatings, those of us who were privileged, and I can even give you the names of the people they beat most often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could give those names to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to myself and my brother Muhamed Bicic, the people who were beaten most were (redacted); Izet Izetbegovic; Dragan Lukac; Ibrahim Salkic, nicknamed Ibro; Mersad Gibic; Safet Hadzialijagic, nicknamed Coner; Omer Nalic. All of them except the ones that I mentioned - maybe I've left someone out - they were the ones who were abused and beaten up most often. Of course I'm talking about the group that was in the room with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand you said there were between 30 of you in that room. That grew to be 40. What sort of facilities did you have in terms of going to the toilet, eating your food, water?

utterances.speaker: HASAN BICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning, we had some food. We would get water in a large canister, can, and it was very often bloody, just like the floor and walls of the room we were in. And as to the other facilities, we would take advantage of the situation. When the guards proved to be less brutal and cruel and if we happened to know some of the guards, we would go to the toilet under their sort of protection, because we were afraid if we went out to the toilet - and this happened - some people on the way to the toilet would be beaten up. So we didn't like to use the toilet very often because of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
